summary: This government bill creates a new Real Estate Business Act. It sets up a Property Regulatory Authority under the housing ministry to license developers, brokers and valuers, register agents and real estate projects, and keep the official freehold and leasehold property registers. It sets rules for selling homes before they are built, with buyers' money held in escrow, and lets owners of residential plots on inhabited islands team up with developers. It also lets the President declare 'Integrated Real Estate Zones' of at least 200 hectares, run by a master developer investing at least USD 1 billion, where property can be sold to foreigners under nationality quotas. It repeals Chapter 7 (strata development) of the Condominium Act (Law No. 33/2021). A few words in the zone service-fee articles (101 to 108) are unclear in the scan.
whyItMatters: People buying a flat from a developer would sign a registered sale agreement, have their payments held in escrow, and could claim compensation or a refund if the project is late. Developers, brokers, agents and valuers would need licences, and a property sale would only be valid once registered with the Authority, with the buyer paying a 3% registration fee.
keyProvisions: Articles 35 to 40 set up the Property Regulatory Authority under the ministry, run by a board the President appoints on the minister's advice for 5-year terms; board members cannot hold shares or posts in real estate companies. Under Articles 42 to 44 a property transaction is valid only once registered, and the buyer pays the Authority 3% of the higher of market value or sale price. Article 63 says such sales no longer need to go through the courts.

Article 48 bans advertising, booking or selling any part of a project before it is registered, and Article 110 requires a separate developer licence for each project, issued only to companies or partnerships registered in the Maldives. Article 51 requires a sale and purchase agreement covering price, payment schedule, handover date, refunds and penalties. Article 54 caps a booking fee or advance at 10% of the price, and Article 55 gives buyers a 21-day option period after receiving the draft agreement.

Article 56 makes developers put off-plan buyers' money into an escrow account at a bank chosen by the Authority, released in stages as building work progresses; 5% is held back until one year after the units are registered to buyers. Escrow and project-account money does not count as the developer's assets if it goes bankrupt, is wound up or loses its licence (Articles 56 and 57). Articles 58 and 59 require compensation for delays and let buyers either take monthly delay penalties or withdraw and get their money back.

Chapter 7 (Articles 69 to 75) lets owners of state or private residential plots on inhabited islands develop them with a developer under a registered development and sales agreement. The landowner must get some units free of charge, leasehold shares must run for 25 to 99 years, neighbouring plots can be combined, and units may only be sold to Maldivians or to entities owned solely by Maldivians.

Chapter 8 (Articles 76 to 109) covers the zones: leased to a master developer for at least 99 years, with a land premium that can be at least 10% of sales, rents and some business income (Article 79). Article 80 sets a 4% registration fee and exempts sale profits from capital gains and non-resident withholding tax; Article 81 taxes goods and services in zones at the tourism GST rate. Article 89 lets properties be sold as 99-year titles re-granted by the Authority, which give no right to citizenship. Article 94 limits any one nationality to 25% of buildings and of residential units (not applying to Maldivians), and Article 93 bans sales to Israeli citizens or companies they hold shares in.

Article 77 bans importing, selling or using alcohol, pork and gambling items in zones, and Article 98 bars gambling businesses and non-Islamic places of worship or religious gatherings there. Brokers, agents and valuers must be at least 21 with no theft or fraud conviction in the last 5 years (Articles 123, 125 and 133), and brokers and agents may not hold clients' money (Article 128). Article 150 sets fines of 10% to 30% of project cost for developers, MVR 100,000 to 1,000,000 for brokers and MVR 50,000 to 500,000 for agents, plus MVR 1,000 a day if unpaid. Complaints go to the Authority, then its review committee, then to court within 30 days.
whoIsAffected: People buying flats or other property from developers, owners of residential plots, real estate developers, brokers, agents and valuers, banks acting as escrow agents, and foreign buyers and master developers in the new zones.
statedReasons: The government says the bill develops the real estate sector sustainably under a transparent and accountable system. It sets rules for registering developers, protects people who buy units in real estate projects, and creates a system to monitor everyone in the business.
